entities.summary: Abū Sahl Bishr ibn al-Muʿtamir ibn Bishr al-Ḥilālī was a Muʿtazilite–Zaydite theologian and founder of the Bishriyya school in Baghdad. Born in 800 CE, he was a student of the prominent theologian, Ahmad ibn ʿUmar al-Waʿizī. His theological contributions had a lasting impact on Islamic thought, particularly in the realms of free will and predestination. The Bishriyya school's emphasis on reason and individual interpretation of the Quran influenced the development of Islamic jurisprudence. Bishr ibn al-Muʿtamir's work, 'The Book of Predestination', is still studied by scholars today. His theological legacy has shaped the intellectual landscape of the Islamic world for centuries. The Bishriyya school's influence can be seen in the works of later Islamic thinkers, such as Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyyah. The school's emphasis on reason and individual interpretation of the Quran also resonated with the intellectual currents of the Abbasid Caliphate's capital, Baghdad. Bishr ibn al-Muʿtamir's work on free will and predestination has been interpreted as a response to the theological debates of the Abbasid era. His contributions to the Bishriyya school have left an enduring mark on the intellectual history of Islam.

entities.summary:
Bischr ibn al-Muʿtamir (800–825 CE) was a pivotal figure in the development of Muʿtazilite–Zaydite theology in Baghdad. As the founder of the Bishriyya school, he played a crucial role in shaping the intellectual landscape of the Islamic Golden Age.









The Bishriyya school's emphasis on reason, free will, and the nature of God had significant implications for Islamic thought and the broader intellectual currents of the time. Ibn al-Muʿtamir's work influenced prominent thinkers such as Al-Shafi'i and Al-Ghazali, shaping the trajectory of Islamic theology for centuries to come.









Bischr ibn al-Muʿtamir's significance extends beyond the realm of theology, as his contributions to the Bishriyya school also had far-reaching impacts on the fields of philosophy, law, and science.









In the context of the Abbasid Caliphate's cultural and intellectual flowering, Ibn al-Muʿtamir's work exemplifies the dynamic interplay between faith, reason, and intellectual curiosity that characterized this pivotal moment in Islamic history.
